sec.title: Background
sec.p: Esketamine has a relatively low adverse effect on mothers and infants during cesarean sections, making it an ideal adjunct in spinal anesthesia. However, its efficacy, dosage, analgesic effects, and safety in preventing postpartum depression (PPD) remain controversial.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science up to January 18, 2024, for studies examining the perioperative use of esketamine to prevent PPD. Two researchers independently assessed studies for eligibility and risk of bias and extracted data on the incidence of PPD and adverse reactions, EPDS scores, and postoperative pain scores. The study protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024527906).

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: Of the 214 studies identified, ten (one retrospective study and nine randomized controlled trials) were selected through full-text reading, involving a total of 1975 cases. The PPD incidence within 1 week after childbirth in the esketamine group was significantly lower than that in the control group (RR = 0·49, 95% CI: 0·30 to 0·79, P = 0·004). The score of Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) within 1 week postpartum was also significantly lower in the esketamine group (SMD = -1·10, 95% CI: -1·67 to -0·52, P < 0·0005). The pain scores during activity and rest, obtained 48 h postoperatively, showed a significant reduction in the esketamine group.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: Perioperative use of esketamine during cesarean section can prevent the early occurrence of PPD while providing effective analgesia. Our findings may guide the clinical use of esketamine for PPD prevention.

sec.title: Evidence before this study
sec.p: Esketamine is a commonly used analgesic that is twice as potent as ketamine. Multiple isolated clinical trials have examined the clinical efficacy of esketamine administered at different dosages and timing. However, no meta-analysis has systematically combined all available high-quality evidence to understand the effects of esketamine comprehensively.

sec.title: Added value of this study
sec.p: This meta-analysis includes nine randomized control trials and one retrospective study comprising 1975 participants. It embarks on a first-of-its-kind analysis to demonstrate the evidence supporting the routine use of esketamine in obstetric anesthesia. Data on the effect and the dosing combination, as well as the time-course response, were provided.

sec.title: Implications of all the available evidence
sec.p: The perioperative use of esketamine during cesarean section can prevent the occurrence of PPD while providing effective analgesia, with no increase in adverse reactions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common mood disorder in postpartum women characterized by depressive symptoms such as depressive mood, anxiety, irritability, fear, pessimism, lack of excitement, and limited coping abilities [1]. PPD can occur in women experiencing childbirth for the first time and those who have given birth multiple times, with a global prevalence rate of 3·5–33% and rates in China of 1.0–52.1% [2, 3]. Most cases of PPD likely occur within the first week postpartum, peaking at 6 weeks postpartum [4], with reports indicating that 24% of cases persist for over 1 year [5]. PPD can significantly impact maternal recovery and delay the growth and development of infants owing to the deteriorated mother-infant relationships. In severe cases, PPD may lead to maternal suicide, which accounts for about 20% of postpartum maternal deaths [6]. Currently, the clinical treatment of PPD primarily involves a combination of psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy, but research suggests that the long-term effect of drug treatment adversely affects infants’ cognitive, behavioral, neural, and emotional development [7, 8]. Therefore, the prevention of PPD is paramount; however, the underlying mechanisms of PPD remain unclear.

Possible etiological factors for PPD include trauma, pain, endocrine changes, psychological stress, and social factors [9]. A previous study suggests that post-cesarean section pain is associated with the early onset of PPD [10]. Moreover, postoperative pain can interfere with milk secretion, delay breastfeeding, and reduce intimate mother-infant interactions [11], suggesting that effective analgesia is a mechanism for preventing PPD.

Esketamine is an antagonist of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR). It is approximately twice as potent as ketamine at the receptor site [11]. Esketamine has been a promising option for treating depression [12–19]. The underlying mechanisms are detailed below. First, esketamine exerts antidepressant effects by blocking NMDARs and activating AMPA receptors [20]. Second, it targets the monoaminergic system, causing norepinephrine (NE) to move from the plasma membrane to the cytoplasm, reducing serum NE and epinephrine levels [21]. Third, esketamine may alleviate tension and depression through interactions between the glutamate system and leptin receptors [22]. In addition, it can enhance neuroplasticity and synaptogenesis [23]. Finally, esketamine produces antidepressant effects by blocking the activity of γ-aminobutyric acid [24]. Recent animal studies suggest that esketamine exerts antidepressant effects by reducing the levels of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α), apoptotic factors, and autophagy markers [25].

Esketamine has a relatively low adverse effect profile on mothers or infants during cesarean sections [26], making it an ideal adjunct in spinal anesthesia. It achieves postoperative sedation, has an analgesic effect, and prevents PPD [27]. However, its clinical efficacy, dosage, and safety in preventing PPD remain controversial. In this meta-analysis, we systematically reviewed the literature to explore the impact of perioperative use of esketamine on postpartum depression and the incidence of adverse events.

sec.title: Retrieval strategies
sec.p: This meta-analysis was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. We searched PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science from inception to January 18, 2024. The following terms were used: “cesarean section”, “pregnancy”, “delivery”, “esketamine”, “postpartum depressive symptoms”, “PPD”, “postpartum depression”, and “Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)”. For instance, the search strategy employed on PubMed is as follows: “Esketamine” [Title/Abstract] AND (“postpartum depres*” [Title/Abstract] OR “EPDS” [Title/Abstract]).

sec.title: Inclusion criteria
sec.p: The study was designed as randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or prospective or retrospective cohort studies; Study participants included pregnant women planning to undergo cesarean section; The experimental group received perioperative intravenous esketamine, while the control group received perioperative intravenous normal saline; Outcome measures included the incidence or scores of PPD in postpartum women; The study must be published in English.

sec.title: Exclusion criteria
sec.p: Duplicate publications: studies that have been previously published elsewhere were excluded from consideration; Studies with incomplete data: research studies lacking comprehensive data were excluded to ensure the integrity and reliability of the data.

sec.title: Literature screening and data extraction
sec.p: Two researchers screened the literature by reviewing the titles and abstracts according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Articles that potentially met the criteria were selected for full-text reading. Where a discrepancy existed, discussions were held, and a third researcher made the final judgment. The data extraction included the following information: author names, publication dates, participants’ mean age, sample size, timing of esketamine administration, dosage, anesthesia method for cesarean section, postoperative pain management method, incidence of PPD, PPD scores, postoperative pain scores, and rate of adverse reactions. The occurrence of PPD was primarily assessed using the EPDS, where a total score of 10 or higher indicates the presence of PPD. In cases where data were not provided, attempts were made to contact the authors for the original data or extract data from figures using software such as PlotDigitizer.

sec.title: Quality assessment
sec.p: Two researchers independently assessed RCTs utilizing the Revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB2) in the Cochrane Handbook. The main indicators included the randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, selective outcome reporting, and overall risk. Retrospective studies were assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale including three dimensions and eight items. The highest score is 9 points, with scores below 5 indicating low-quality studies. Consistent conclusions were reached after a discussion between the two researchers. In cases of disagreement, a third party makes the final judgment.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: We extracted data such as authors, publication time, age, sample size, esketamine application, dosage, method of anesthesia for cesarean section, postoperative analgesia method, postoperative PPD incidence rate, EPDS scores, postoperative pain scores, and incidence rate of adverse reactions. Dosages were categorized into high (> 0.25/kg) and low (≤ 0.25 mg/kg) dose groups; timing of esketamine administration was divided as follows: during surgery (Subgroup A), post-surgery using an analgesia pump (Subgroup B), and both during and post-surgery with an analgesia pump (Subgroup C). The primary outcome was the incidence rate of PPD, assessed mainly using the EPDS. An EPDS total score of 30, with scores above 9 indicating the presence of PPD. Secondary outcomes included EPDS scores, postoperative pain scoring, and incidence of adverse reactions. Postoperative pain scoring during rest and activity within 48 h post-surgery was mainly evaluated using the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) for pain. Subgroup analysis was also conducted according to the dosage and timing of esketamine administration.

Meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager 5.4 and Stata 17.0 software. The heterogeneity among the included studies was assessed using the I2 test. If I2 was equal to or greater than 50%, the heterogeneity was considered significant, and a random-effects model was used for analysis. If I2 was less than 50%, the heterogeneity was considered not significant, and a fixed-effects model was therefore used. Relative risks (RR) and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated for dichotomous variables. For continuous variables, standardized mean differences (SMD) and their 95% CIs were calculated. Subgroup analysis and sensitivity analysis were performed to investigate potential sources of heterogeneity. Potential publication bias was estimated using Egger’s linear regression test, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Role of the funding source
sec.p: There was no funding source for this study. All authors had access to all meta-analyzed data used in this study and accepted responsibility for the decision to submit the manuscript for publication.

sec.p: All studies adhered to the intended interventions.

sec.title: Missing outcome data
sec.p: One study had insufficient data for outcome variables (< 95%), resulting in an “unclear risk of bias.”

sec.title: Outcome measurement and selective outcome reporting
sec.p: All the studies were classified as low risk of bias.

sec.title: Overall risk
sec.p: Six studies were rated as low risk, while three were as “unclear risk of bias.”

sec.p:
Seven studies reported adverse reactions, like postoperative nausea and vomiting, headache, dizziness, nightmares, and skin itching. As seen in Fig. 8, no significant difference was noted in the occurrence of vomiting between the esketamine and control groups (RR = 0·79, 95% CI: 0·52 to 1·20, P = 0·27 > 0·05) using the random-effects model (I2 = 56%). Among the four studies assessing the occurrence of headache and dizziness (Fig. 9), the esketamine group exhibited a significantly higher rate than the control group (RR = 1·37, 95% CI: 1·02 to 1·85, P = 0·04 < 0·05). Additionally, three studies reported the occurrences of nightmares (Fig. 10) and itchy skin (Fig. 11) respectively, and found no significant difference between the groups (RR = 0·98, 95% CI: 0·23 to 4·22, P = 0·98 > 0·05; RR = 1·00, 95% CI: 0·49 to 2·04, P = 1·00 > 0·05, respectively).Fig. 8

sec.title: Pain score 48 h postoperatively
sec.p:
Among the included studies, three reported pain scores during activity and at rest 48 h postoperatively. As shown in Figs. 12 and 13, using a random-effects model, the activity and rest pain scores at 48 h post-operation were substantially decreased in the esketamine group (during activity: SMD = −0·32, 95% CI: −0.48 to −0.16, P = 0·0001 < 0·05; at rest: SMD = −0·34, 95% CI: −0·50 to −0·17, P < 0·0001).Fig. 12

sec.title: Subgroup analysis based on differences in esketamine dosage
sec.p: Subgroup analyses of outcomes were conducted based on differences in esketamine dosage.

As shown in Fig. 14, in the subgroup receiving high (> 0·25 mg/kg) esketamine doses, the incidence of PPD within one week after childbirth was significantly lower compared to the control group (RR = 0·48, 95% CI: 0·29 to 0·80, P = 0·005 < 0·05). Meanwhile, in the subgroup receiving low (≤ 0·25 mg/kg) esketamine doses, there was no significant difference in the incidence of PPD compared to the control group (RR = 0·38, 95% CI: 0·10 to 1·40, P = 0·15 > 0·05).Fig. 14
Subgroup analysis of incidence rate of PPD within 1 week postpartum according to esketamine dosages

Similarly, in the subgroup receiving high esketamine doses, the EPDS scores within the first week after childbirth was significantly lower compared to the control group (RR = −0·42, 95% CI: −0·58 to −0·26, P < 0·00001). However, in the subgroup receiving esketamine doses of 0·25 mg/kg or less, there was no significant difference (RR = −0·22, 95% CI: −0·61 to 0·16, P = 0·26 > 0·05), as shown in Fig. 15.Fig. 15
Subgroup analysis of EPDS scores within 1 week postpartum according to esketamine dosages

sec.title: Subgroup analysis based on different timing of esketamine administration
sec.p:
Subgroup analyses were conducted based on different timing of esketamine administration. As shown in Fig. 16, in the subgroup of participants receiving intravenous esketamine injection during surgery (Subgroup A) (RR = 0·60, 95% CI: 0·24 to 1·47, P = 0·26 > 0·05) and those using only an analgesic pump post-surgery (Subgroup B) (RR = 0·47, 95% CI: 0·16 to 1·43, P = 0·19 > 0·05), the incidence of PPD within the first week after childbirth was similar to that in the control group. However, in the subgroup of participants utilizing a combination of intravenous esketamine intraoperatively and esketamine-containing analgesic pump postoperatively (Subgroup C) (RR = 0·49, 95% CI: 0·30 to 0·79, P = 0·002 < 0·05), the incidence of PPD within one week postpartum was significantly lower compared to the control group.Fig. 16
Subgroup analysis of the incidence rate of PPD within 1 week postpartum based on timing of administration. A Intravenous injection during cesarean section. B Analgesic pump containing esketamine for continuous 48 h postpartum administration. C A + B

As for the EPDS scores within the first week postpartum, in the subgroup of participants receiving intravenous esketamine injection during surgery (Subgroup A) (RR = −0·27, 95% CI: −0·96 to 0·42, P = 0·45 > 0·05) and those utilizing a combination intravenous esketamine intraoperatively and esketamine-containing analgesic pump postoperatively (Subgroup C) (RR = −0·15, 95% CI: −0·51 to 0·20, P = 0·39 > 0·05), there was no significant difference compared to the control group, as shown in Fig. 17. Meanwhile, in the subgroup using only analgesic pump post-surgery (Subgroup B) (RR = −0·49, 95% CI: −0·64 to −0·33, P < 0·00001), the EPDS scores within the first week postpartum was significantly lower compared to the control group.Fig. 17

sec.title: Subgroup analysis of incidence rate of headache and dizziness according to esketamine dosages
sec.p: A subgroup analysis of the incidence rates of headache and dizziness was conducted based on the differences in the dosage of esketamine.

As shown in Fig. 18, in the subgroup receiving high doses (> 0.25 mg/kg) of esketamine, the incidence rate of headache and dizziness was significantly lower than that in the control group (RR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.02 to 1.86, P = 0.004 < 0.05). Meanwhile, in the subgroup receiving low doses (≤ 0.25 mg/kg) of esketamine, there was no significant difference in the incidence rate of headache and dizziness compared with the control group (RR = 3.00, CI: 0.32 to 28.27, P = 0.34 > 0.05).Fig. 18

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p:
To explore the potential sources of heterogeneity, this study conducted a sensitivity analysis of the incidence rate and scores of PPD within the first week after childbirth. The results showed that even after excluding any single study, the direction of the pooled effect size and its statistical significance did not change significantly, indicating a high degree of consistency and reliability of the results (Figs. 19 and 20).Fig. 19

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our meta-analysis of existing studies examined the perioperative use of esketamine in the prevention of PPD after cesarean section. Our data show that perioperative use of esketamine significantly reduces PPD incidence and EPDS scores within the first week postpartum. However, this effect does not persist up to 4–6 weeks postpartum. The perioperative use of esketamine can reduce the pain score at 48 h after surgery. Intravenous administration of esketamine during the operation and the use of an analgesic pump containing esketamine after the operation will produce a better antidepressant effect. Apart from a higher rate of headaches and dizziness in the esketamine group, other adverse reactions, such as nausea and vomiting, nightmares, and itchy skin, were generally consistent with those in the control group.

Esketamine is a S-enantiomer of ketamine. The antidepressant effects of ketamine can last for 3–7 days, leading to the speculation that its main metabolite, nor-ketamine, also possesses antidepressant effects [38]. Given that most cases of PPD occur within the first week and the sixth week postpartum [39], our data suggest that perioperative esketamine in patients undergoing cesarean section can reduce the incidence and severity of PPD within the first week postpartum. Although there was reduced PPD incidence and severity at 4–6 weeks postpartum in the esketamine group, the difference did not reach the statistical significance, consistent with the metabolic lifespan of esketamine in the body. A recent meta-analysis indicated that esketamine could improve the incidence of PPD at 42 days [40]. This analysis included articles in both English and Chinese, with a publication deadline of April 1, 2023, and a sample size of 1288. Our study included only articles published in English, with a search cutoff date of January 18, 2024. The discrepancies between these two sets of results could be due to differences in race, timing, and sample size.

Studies have shown that a single intravenous dose of ketamine 0·5 mg/kg can significantly relieve symptoms of depression within 40–60 min, with antidepressant effects lasting 5–8 h [41]. Esketamine has a greater affinity for NMDARs than ketamine and provides analgesic effects approximately 1·5–2 times stronger [42, 43]. Moreover, it requires only half the dose of ketamine to achieve the same effect. Our subgroup analysis indicates that a higher dose (> 0·25 mg/kg) of esketamine can reduce the incidence of PPD, achieving an equivalent effect to ketamine (0·5 mg/kg). According to the results of the subgroup analysis, there are significant differences in the effectiveness of esketamine in preventing postpartum depression due to different administration timings and methods. This study found that intravenous injection during the operation combined with continuous infusion through an analgesic pump for 48 h after the operation (Group C) can reduce the incidence of PPD one week after childbirth by 51%, while single administration during the operation alone (Group A) or infusion only through the postoperative analgesic pump (Group B) did not reach statistical significance. It is worth noting that Group B showed a significant advantage in terms of the improvement of the EPDS scores, suggesting that continuous infusion may enhance the antidepressant effect by maintaining a stable blood drug concentration. Future studies need to further explore the optimal combination of the intraoperative loading dose and postoperative continuous infusion, and evaluate its long-term impact on the neurodevelopment of both mothers and infants.

Compared to opioids, esketamine does not significantly suppress respiration, making it suitable for pediatric and obstetric anesthesia, as well as adjunctive analgesia [44]. From a clinical practical perspective, the mechanism of action of continuous infusion of esketamine at subanesthetic doses (0.1–0.5 mg/kg) deserves special attention. By selectively blocking NMDA receptors, this administration method effectively inhibits the overactivation of ascending nociceptive pathways, thereby reducing the release of pain-inducing substances (such as bradykinin and substance P) at the spinal cord level [45–47]. It is worth noting that this low-dose regimen should not be simply categorized as a traditional"analgesic". First, it has significant"antihyperalgesic"effects, which can prevent and reverse central sensitization. Second, it exhibits clear"antiallodynic"effects and has unique efficacy against neuropathic pain components. Most importantly, this administration method can provide"tolerance protection,"effectively delaying the development of opioid tolerance, which is particularly important for patients requiring long-term analgesia [48, 49]. In clinical practice, this administration strategy is particularly suitable for patients expected to experience severe postoperative pain, those with a history of chronic pain or at risk of hyperalgesia, and cases requiring long-term opioid use; a continuous infusion regimen of 48–72 h is recommended, with individualized adjustments made based on patient response and side effects such as psychiatric symptoms and blood pressure changes. A meta-analysis indicated that esketamine could significantly reduce postpartum pain scores at 48 h, consistent with our findings. While the perioperative use of esketamine in cesarean sections to mitigate the risk of PPD may be related to its analgesic effect [44], further extensive clinical research is required to validate this conclusion.

To date, the tolerance and safety of intravenous esketamine treatment for depression have received considerable attention owing to its various adverse reactions. This meta-analysis compiled the common side effects of routinely using esketamine to prevent PPD, including nausea and vomiting, headaches, dizziness, nightmares, and itchy skin. The results indicate that the esketamine group had a relatively higher incidence of headaches and dizziness compared to the control group, but there was no significant difference in the incidence of other adverse events. A recent meta-analysis on the PPD prevention of ketamine and esketamine showed a significantly higher incidence of postoperative adverse events (e.g., headaches, dizziness, double vision, and hallucinations) in the experimental group than in the control group [50]. The common side effects of esketamine are dissociative symptoms, dizziness, somnolence, nausea and vomiting, elevated blood pressure, and increased heart rate. These side effects are usually mild, transient, and self-limiting [51–54]. As for repeated esketamine infusions, many experts have raised concerns regarding the risks of urotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, cognitive deficits, and dependency observed with high doses of esketamine use (recreational use or the management of chronic pain) [51].

To ensure the safe use of medications, we recommend excluding pregnant women with psychiatric disorders, glaucoma, moderate-to-severe hypertension, intracranial hypertension, congestive heart failure, or a history of cerebrovascular disease or substance abuse. Fasting for 6–8 h before esketamine infusion and using antiemetic drugs (e.g., ondansetron) for nausea control and non-prescription analgesics for moderate-to-severe headaches are effective [55]. Furthermore, a low rate of esketamine infusion can reduce opioid consumption and postoperative delirium [52, 56].

The occurrence of anxiety and depression results from multifactorial interactions, with prolonged PPD showing a lower response to traditional antidepressants. The articles referenced in this study predominantly involve single or low doses of esketamine administration. The effects of multiple or high doses of esketamine on mothers and infants require further extensive research. Although most cases can resolve within a few months, approximately 24% of cases persist for over a year, with no studies evaluating whether esketamine can decrease the prevalence of PPD 1 year postpartum.

Research on the application of ketamine in newborns is underway. Ketamine is known to be toxic to the newborn brain [57], and its metabolites can be absorbed through breast milk. Extensive animal studies have demonstrated that ketamine could induce dose-dependent neurodegeneration in the developing brain of rodents. Some preclinical studies of post-birth have demonstrated that ketamine can lead to apoptosis and brain damage in young rodents [58–60]. However, the evidence is lacking regarding the neurological effects of esketamine on the newborn brain, warranting further clinical studies [50–52].

Several limitations must be acknowledged in the present analysis. First, the included sample size is relatively small, which may limit generalizability to a broader population. However, the number of clinical trials regarding this research has been continuously increasing recently, and it will be continually updated to provide the latest data. Second, the range of drug dosages included in this review is 0.1–1.25 mg/kg. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to high- and low-dosage groups, but the wide span of the high-dosage group (0.25–1.25 mg/kg) may introduce certain risks of bias. Third, among the secondary outcome measures, only three studies were included for nightmares and skin itching in postoperative adverse reactions. Similarly, only three studies were included for the 48-h NRS pain score. The limited number of included studies may affect the accuracy of the results. Additionally, we only included literature published in English, excluding publications in other languages and gray literature. In the future, it is necessary to include studies in multiple languages and conduct sensitivity analyses to assess the potential impact of literature in different languages on the results.

In conclusion, perioperative use of esketamine can reduce the incidence and severity of PPD within one week, and it will not increase the occurrences of nausea, vomiting, nightmares, and skin itching. However, it may increase the incidences of headache and dizziness.
